p: Thank you, Chair. And congratulations on your nomination. You know, part of my questions will be hyper-local and then spread out. In communities like East New York and Brownsville, especially the Nehemiah houses, residents are concerned about the overdevelopment and the losing of character and identity of neighborhoods that were built for working class homeowners. How do you see the LPC working with communities like the Nehemiah, East New York, Brownsville, and New Lots to help preserve neighborhood character while still allowing for smart and thoughtful growth without changing the character of the community?

It's a great question. And, you know, when an area is, say, like undergoing a rezoning or plan for growth, we do try and partner with City Planning to look at the preservation opportunities. You know, in fact, in East New York,

COMMITTEE ON RULES, PRIVILEGES, ELECTIONS, STANDARDS AND ETHICS 48 we did designate the Empire State Dairy on Atlantic Avenue that has the new development behind it.
Correct. Yes.

And, yeah, we crafted the designation to keep the front building, but then to allow the housing to be built behind it. So, I thought that was a creative way to both have the preservation and, you know, the new housing. But, you know, our job is to protect historic character, not necessarily to stop change. But I understand that, you know, when there is change and when there's new development that it can be upsetting to people.
Right.

I think, you know, we do want to make sure that we are looking at potential designations in those areas that are experiencing change. You know, we've done surveys in East New York. I think there's still interesting resources out there. I'm happy to talk to you.

Okay. Well, we'd definitely love to have more conversation on that. One thing we hear often from communities is that conversations around landmarking usually happen after development have already started and

COMMITTEE ON RULES, PRIVILEGES, ELECTIONS, STANDARDS AND ETHICS 49 residents feel like, you know, like they're playing catch up. As the Commissioner, would you support early engagement with communities and more proactive approach to identifying neighborhoods with historical or cultural significance before they are heavily impacted by development?

Yeah. And, you know, we, again, working with City Planning, you know, recently with the Midtown South rezoning, for example, we designated five important historic resources in advance of that rezoning. And, you know, I think that we looked at places that were both historically and culturally significant, but also had what we call it placemaking, you know, that had a real presence in the neighborhood, that their preservation would help retain that character of the area while it also was undergoing some redevelopment. So, I think that's, you know, that's something that's important to me. We've done that with various rezonings in the Gowanus Rezoning, we did that as well. We designated five buildings there too. So, you know, I think it's good planning to sort of bring the preservation and planning issues together. So, happy to continue to do that when it's appropriate.

COMMITTEE ON RULES, PRIVILEGES, ELECTIONS, STANDARDS AND ETHICS 50

Thank you. Thank you for your response on that. As you know, many NYCHA residents across the city, including in my District, which has about 12 NYCHA developments, have concerns about the long-term future of public housing under this Administration and its continued push to privatize developments or place developments into the RAD-PACT program. Residents are concerned not only about management changes from NYCHA to private managers, but also about preserving the identity, the history, and the community fabric, which these developments over time, as we've seen a conversion surrounding places like Fulton-Chelsea-Elliott, for example, where they are looking to completely demolish that development. What role, if any, do you believe the LPC can play in helping preserve historically and culturally significant public housing communities as conversions and around redevelopment and modernization of NYCHA continues?

Sure. I mean, we have designated two NYCHA complexes, you know, and I think what we've really looked at with those is kind of the first sort of the prototypes of the housing. One is

COMMITTEE ON RULES, PRIVILEGES, ELECTIONS, STANDARDS AND ETHICS 51 Williamsburg housing and the other one, I'm forgetting the name in Harlem. And so really looking at some of the earliest housing too, that kind of embodies that type.
Right.

You know, and I think that those were important designations for us, important for the city. You know, I'm not necessarily sure that we would be looking at more designations of NYCHA since we've done these really important ones. You know, so I know, you know, there's some that are on the national register and they're able to use federal historic tax credits, which is very important. So, we've played a small role in that review process, but I think the designations we've done are great and important. And we've been happy to work with NYCHA as they improved those two designations.

Okay. NYCHA developments are home to generations of New Yorkers and represent an important part of the city's social and cultural history, especially for Black and Brown communities and working-class families. Do you believe there should be broader conversations around

COMMITTEE ON RULES, PRIVILEGES, ELECTIONS, STANDARDS AND ETHICS 52 recognizing the historical and cultural significance of certain NYCHA campuses or public housing communities, even if preservation looks different from the traditional landmarking?
It's a great question. And I do think there's very important history there. And I think that the right tool potentially is the one that's being used, which is the National Register.
Right.

There's been important history documented that is actually ongoing. And I think that puts it into the formal record that this history is very, very important, very interesting, you know, public housing, you know, and how it has supported New Yorkers is so important.
Right.

And so I think that that tool that's being used is actually the right one. You know, I'm not sure that necessarily the regulatory arm of LPC is necessarily necessary, but I think documenting that history, the way it's being done now is very important.

Okay.

COMMITTEE ON RULES, PRIVILEGES, ELECTIONS, STANDARDS AND ETHICS 53 One concern I hear often from residents is that redevelopment conversations can sometimes happen to communities instead of with communities. And from your perspective, how can the LPC help ensure residents have a stronger voice in conversations about preserving public housing, working class, Black and Brown neighborhoods, when it comes to preserving the identity and also looking at the community history before major development decisions are made. And, while I also understand that the, you know, the City's pushed for more housing, we also have to make sure that we're protecting the OG, which I call the oldest affordable housing stock in the City of New York, which is NYCHA, and not selling it out. So, I just want to kind of get your perspective of what the LPC would do in those situations.

Yeah. I mean, I think it's hard for LPC when, unless it's actually designated by us, we don't necessarily have a role. I agree that those conversations are really important to have. You know, when we did do review proposed work on the two that we have designated, we did have

COMMITTEE ON RULES, PRIVILEGES, ELECTIONS, STANDARDS AND ETHICS 54 community testimony and that's a very important part of our process.
Right.

But, you know, I think that those conversations, I think there's people in the City really good at running those kinds of conversations. I'm not sure how much we would have to add unless they're actually designated.
Is there a list that exists of all the designated NYCHA developments?
Yes. And we're happy to provide that to you.
Okay.
I'm sorry that I don't have a top of mind, but we can provide that.

Once you hopefully, once you become Chair, you can provide that. And my last question pertains to Thomas Jefferson High School, which there's been some controversy around a particular statue of Thomas Jefferson that is placed in the hallway of Thomas Jefferson High School, and there's been multiple petitions that have been circulated by the students of Thomas Jefferson. Now it's a campus because it's

COMMITTEE ON RULES, PRIVILEGES, ELECTIONS, STANDARDS AND ETHICS 55 made up of multiple high schools asking that the statue be removed, and this is from their own knowledge and studying the history. So, we know that the statue has been stated to us by DOE that the statue is landmarked. We would love to work with you to see how we can acquiesce to the wishes and the desires of the students who wish to have that statue removed from the hallway.
I'm happy to talk about it. I'm not familiar with the situation. You know, if this is a statue that say attached to the building or it's just a statue…

It's a statue right in the hallway. As soon as you walk into the building, it's a big Thomas Jefferson statue, but it was stated to us by a DOE that the statue is landmarked. So, there were conversations around covering the statue up or removal of the statue. And again, I just want to say that this is something that came from the students who said that they didn't want that statue in their hallways. They have to walk past it as they're going to class.

Yeah. If it's on the interior and it is an individual landmark, I'm not

COMMITTEE ON RULES, PRIVILEGES, ELECTIONS, STANDARDS AND ETHICS 56 quite sure, but if it's on the interior, I don't think that we would regulate it at all actually.
There's no regulation?
But we can look into that to confirm that. I probably shouldn't say that.
So interior landmarking, who would that go through?
So, we have about 120 interior landmarks across the city. They're very rare. I don't know that we have any high schools that have interior landmarks. I could be wrong about that.
Right.

But typically when we've designated school buildings, we don't do the interior as well. So, and even if it is a monument on the outside, you know, we have approved removals of certain monuments. Sometimes we don't regulate them. It depends. But we could certainly look into this some more.

That's what we want. We want folks to get information back to us that's accurate. But according to the DOE, they're saying that it's landmarked.

COMMITTEE ON RULES, PRIVILEGES, ELECTIONS, STANDARDS AND ETHICS 57
Okay. We can look into it.
Thank you. Thank you, Madam Chair.

Thank you. We've also been joined by Council Member Brewer. I do have a few more questions and then I'll turn it over to Council Member Brewer. At the last hearing, the Council held on nominations for the LPC, a number of advocates testified that they hoped the LPC would deny the West Park Presbyterian request for approval to demolish their landmark building so that the site can be sold to a residential developer. What is the current status of the application?

So, this is a hardship application and it is before the Commission now. And like I said, hardship applications are very rare and they are a fact-driven process. And so, you know, as this is something I could potentially be voting on if I weren't nominated or approved, you know, I have to be careful about what I say. But I can assure you that this is going through a very robust review.

COMMITTEE ON RULES, PRIVILEGES, ELECTIONS, STANDARDS AND ETHICS 58 We've had a public hearing. We've had two public meetings. We've had lots of documents submitted to us, both from the applicant and from individuals, from organizations, from elected officials. So, this is undergoing a very careful review.

Thank you. So, you know, let's just take this broadly, right? So, in this case, the church claims it's a hardship to maintain its current building and they said they will use the expected funds from the sales to start a social justice fund. So, without saying it's West Park, this current application, what do you think about in general when, you know, churches have these hardship applications?

Well, you know, there's been so few hardship applications, you know, there's been 23, I think, you know, over the history of the Commission so they're very rare and each one is different and each one is fact-driven. So, I'm not sure that I can necessarily compare one to another. You know, I would say just generally with faith-based organizations, you know, we are sympathetic to their needs. You know, they sometimes have buildings that are expensive to maintain. They've experienced

COMMITTEE ON RULES, PRIVILEGES, ELECTIONS, STANDARDS AND ETHICS 59 deferred maintenance. You know, they want to put money into their mission, not necessarily their building sometimes. So, these raise complex issues for the agency that we're very mindful of.
So, what degree of financial hardship should allow a property to be exempt from the Landmark Law?

So, for hardship application, you know, it is prescribed in the law, you know, there's a judicial test, and so that is not something that the Chair or the Commission, you know, kind of unilaterally looks at. It's really prescribed in a judicial test.

Okay. And you have been involved in landmarking other religious sites that claim landmarking will be a hardship. Is landmarking small churches for dwindling congregations something that is bound to fail? If not, how do you propose to keep churches from claiming hardship and selling their landmark sites to residential developers?

It's a good question. It's a difficult question. You know, in terms of our designations, about 1.5 percent are religious in

COMMITTEE ON RULES, PRIVILEGES, ELECTIONS, STANDARDS AND ETHICS 60 nature so it's a small subset. You know, religious properties are often, you know, in a community, some of the most significant architecture, people are very, whether they're a member of it or, you know, a neighborhood resident, they often are, you know, sort of the unofficial landmarks or sometimes official landmarks of a neighborhood. So, you know, we understand that there's competing issues here. You know, we've worked with many religious institutions across the city to help them. We have a team at LPC that is dedicated to permitting just for religious institutions. We think that's really important because they know the building types really well. They often know the congregations or the institutions that can really help them, and, you know, I think we're sympathetic to these issues and to, in some cases, the congregation is getting smaller. So, you know, and when we think about new designations for religious institutions, you know, we are very careful with those. We do get a lot of requests for evaluation for religious institutions. You know, we prioritize a very small number because we understand that these are, you know, they're facing difficult issues at the moment, but we've also helped religious

COMMITTEE ON RULES, PRIVILEGES, ELECTIONS, STANDARDS AND ETHICS 61 institutions grow too. We've approved new buildings adjacent to churches or in the, you know, on a campus in a recent case, an addition, you know, so we've tried to figure out ways that we can help them be financially stable while also retaining the landmark or historic district building.
Thank you. I do have two more questions, but I'd like to turn it over to Council Member Brewer.

I landmarked that damn church and just want to make it very, very clear, and I will make sure that it is there forever, but thank you for your comments. Just generally about the churches. So, when I was dealing with one other church, St. Paul and St. Andrew, we managed to get the basement where there is a non-profit to be a condo working with OMB. So, my question is just generally, do you have any creative answers? I want these churches, synagogues to survive, not to be torn down. So, my question would be, are there any other ideas you might have to give them funding? I know that we cannot give them, State does, but the City can't give them funding for religious purposes. Are there any other suggestions

COMMITTEE ON RULES, PRIVILEGES, ELECTIONS, STANDARDS AND ETHICS 62 that you have about how to maintain them when they are landmarked? Because the roof on St. Paul is five and a half million. Right now, they're raising the money, and there are certain criteria that OMB demands. If you are giving City money, sometimes the churches and synagogues don't want to abide by those rules. So, it is complicated, but we do have to figure out because they cannot survive without some of the funding.
Yeah. And there's certain state funding. I know that…
State can do it.
Yeah, the State can do it.
ADA ramps, they can do some.

Yeah. And it is a challenging issue, and I think, you know, it depends on the particular resource as well. So, you know, I, I think City of Yes has opened up opportunities for some development if there's a campus or parish ground, you know, there could be additional development. I think that can be important.

COMMITTEE ON RULES, PRIVILEGES, ELECTIONS, STANDARDS AND ETHICS 63
Manhattan doesn't have much of that, but I hear you.

Yeah. It might be more in, in the boroughs that that's an option, but I think that's really important. And we have worked with FBOs on approving, you know, new buildings or other kinds of work, including in Manhattan.
Right. Mount Pleasant on 81st Street. I'm aware.

And Lower East Side as well. So, I think that's really important. You know, the improvements to Federal Historic Tax Credit you know, that could help, I wonder, you know, if there is public-private partnership or syndication of tax credits. Right now, it's not used maybe as much as it could be, but I think that could be potentially an opportunity as well.

Okay. That's a topic that really needs more intense discussion. I feel strongly. Second. The communities, I was able to landmark West End Avenue, 850 buildings, but just generally, because we had the funding in the neighborhood to hire, in this case, Angel Dulcar, to

COMMITTEE ON RULES, PRIVILEGES, ELECTIONS, STANDARDS AND ETHICS 64 do the work. So, my question is, is there funding for other historic districts and neighborhoods that may not be able to raise that kind of money? Because when historic districts come to particularly large ones, they need to have, I think, some background and some work done, and then you can supplement it. So, are you making some effort? I'm very bad. I would landmark historic district the whole city. I say right into the microphone, and I get in a whole bunch of trouble, and I don't care. But the issue is, for me, is how do you get other historic districts and neighborhoods that may not have that kind of resource? What are you doing about that?
And I actually said this before you came in.
I'm sorry. I was at another hearing next door.

I don't think that we need additional resources to do that, and I don't think that communities should feel an obligation to provide that level of information to us. We do have a research department. They can undertake this work. You know, it's always helpful to get information. It's helpful to get…

COMMITTEE ON RULES, PRIVILEGES, ELECTIONS, STANDARDS AND ETHICS 65
So, are you doing work with the communities to say this is a potential historic district, or do they have to come to you? How are we making it clearer to people?

So, for example, we just designated two historic districts in Brooklyn and in Flatbush, and, you know, we came up with the boundaries. We had surveyed in the air before. We resurveyed it. We developed the boundaries. To be honest, you know, there was the community had hoped we would do more but we didn't find that, you know, some of those areas merited, but there's back and forth on this, but really this was work that our research department undertook. Nobody needed to pay anything to do that. I don't think that communities should feel obligated to do that. We're happy to work with the preservation organizations. You know, even if we just get rough boundaries, we can look at that and, you know…

We were told in the past that we needed to come up with funding in order to have at least an initial presentation, but it's good to hear. I would love to see, as time goes on, if you are confirmed that LPC says, let's look

COMMITTEE ON RULES, PRIVILEGES, ELECTIONS, STANDARDS AND ETHICS 66 at, I'm making this up, these 10 areas and let's get going on them. Because, you know, people in Harlem complain correctly that they don't feel that they have enough historic districts. I agree, but they also would need some help in identifying them and hoping… it takes time and money to get those areas designated, all the land all the research. So, you're saying you can do all that?
Well, and I will say that community board did a historic preservation plan and they, you know, identified various districts and we've actually designated, I think, three of the…
Right. Harlem now would like more.
I totally understand.
And I'm with them.
We've worked with them in recent years to do three really important district and really identifying and those social justice and civil…

And the 158 houses. I'd still like to get them historic district. I'm just saying, okay. Would you be a loud voice, I hope, I think you said so in your testimony about the

COMMITTEE ON RULES, PRIVILEGES, ELECTIONS, STANDARDS AND ETHICS 67 notion that affordable housing versus landmarking is not a good scenario that we feel that they go together, that you can have affordable housing and it can be landmarked. Is that something that you would talk about?
Well, I think…
I don't like that scenario.

Yes-and answer for that but, you know, I do think that the preservation of buildings can also lead to preservation of affordable units, but I also think that it's really important that we create new housing as well. So I think it's both, and I think that we need to, you know, think about how can we add new housing in historic districts as well.

Okay. Because I would tell you in some cases, people think that you know, you are destroying communities if you have a landmarking and I, or historic districts, and I totally disagree with that. A plaque program. That's obviously Barbara Diamond, Steve, she's been doing that for years. I have a bill in this Council that would love

COMMITTEE ON RULES, PRIVILEGES, ELECTIONS, STANDARDS AND ETHICS 68 to have more plaques on buildings and so on to designate historic culturally or architecturally. Is that something that you would support? Do you have any thoughts about that?

Yes. Well, so the New York Landmarks Preservation Foundation has a plaque program, but then other organizations have plaque programs as well and to steal a pun from our General Counsel, you know, we are mindful of plaque buildup on some buildings that we don't want to have multiple plaques.
No, I'm not saying a lot of… there's a lot of places that there are no plaques at all, you know?

Certainly. I mean, our, our staff regularly approves them, you know, and we help with the Foundation's the text of the plaque and, you know, other information for them, but otherwise, you know, individual property owners come to us all the time ae approve plaque placements regularly.

You probably talked about this earlier, but is there a backlog in terms of, like, how long does it take if a building

COMMITTEE ON RULES, PRIVILEGES, ELECTIONS, STANDARDS AND ETHICS 69 comes to you and it would be hopefully designated and there's a proposal? Obviously, if there's concerns, as there are with the church, that's different. But for a normal… I live in a historic district, my District office is in a historic district. If I could interior my house, I would make that a landmark inside, but I was told I couldn't do that. I renovated right back to 1896, and there's nothing different than 1896. Looks just like it. All the holes and everything. So, my question is, what is a backlog if somebody wants to have, you know, there's a designate or hope for a designation? How long does it take? I mean, obviously, it's average.

Yeah. I wouldn't say that we have a backlog. You know, I think for the actual designation process from the, you know, the calendaring to the designation, you know, we've been moving quite efficiently. Usually, an individual landmark takes three months to six months, and a district probably somewhere between four months and a year, which is well below what the law requires us to do. You know, in terms of, you know, something, what we have prioritized, you know, we're constantly studying buildings across the city. We don't have an

COMMITTEE ON RULES, PRIVILEGES, ELECTIONS, STANDARDS AND ETHICS 70 application process for designations so there's not necessarily a measurable time between, say, if somebody puts in a request for evaluation to when we actually designate something, if it merits, because there's a lot of process of what we're prioritizing. You know, we're trying to also really look at equitable designations across all five boroughs. So, something may merit designation, but we don't necessarily prioritize it, you know, at a given time. So, it's not really measurable. It depends.
Okay. Thank you very much, but I am going to make sure that church survives. Thank you.
Understood.
Thank you. I only have two more questions.
Okay.

LPC has designated some historic sites that have unremarkable aesthetic features, such as the James Baldwin House. Also, refused to designate other sites that hold historic significance for certain communities because they lack high architectural distinctions, such as St. Elizabeth Church on Upper East Side. Doesn't the

COMMITTEE ON RULES, PRIVILEGES, ELECTIONS, STANDARDS AND ETHICS 71 requirement that some historical sites have high architectural distinctions, while not requiring the same of others, illustrate that LPC standards, the very least, are subjectively applied?

Thank you for that question. And, you know, I think it's an important one. You know, the James Baldwin House, I think, is an incredibly important designation and, while it's not architecturally distinguished, it does reflect the time that James Baldwin lived there. He purchased the property when it was basically a row house that was converted to a multifamily house and stripped at a certain point. And so, it reflects the time that he purchased the property. He lived there, his family lived there. He talked about the property being important to him. And so, because it has this strong connection to him and his productive time, we felt it met our criteria for designation. It was an important designation to reflect Black history and also LGBTQ history. So to me, that is an important designation on the Upper West Side. You know, I understand when we don't, for church buildings or for religious institution buildings, you know, they are often quite lovely

COMMITTEE ON RULES, PRIVILEGES, ELECTIONS, STANDARDS AND ETHICS 72 buildings, and so we do have a higher standard for those buildings and we don't necessarily prioritize as many religious institutions for designations. So, you know, it's hard to compare the two buildings, but I think that the James Baldwin, we don't designate many buildings related to a person. That to us was a very important designation.
Okay. I'll just end it with in 11 years, since you joined LPC, have you found that the public is more or less skeptical of the LPC's decisions?

You know, I love New York and I love New Yorkers and, you know, I think there's a healthy skepticism you know, for everything that happens in the city. So, you know, I think that, you know, we have an outsized impact in the city. There's an outsized interest in New York City's historic buildings. People care a lot about the places they live and what it looks like. So I don't know that it's changed much, but I welcome, you know, all kinds of opinions from New Yorkers.

You're indeed a group of diverse opinions.

COMMITTEE ON RULES, PRIVILEGES, ELECTIONS, STANDARDS AND ETHICS 73 I would like to thank you for joining us today and providing your testimony. You are now excused. I will now open up the floor to public for comments. If you wish to speak, please fill the appearance card with the Sergeant-at-Arms and wait to be recognized. We ask that you please limit your comments to two minutes and, if you have a written statement, please provide a copy of that statement to the Sergeant-at-Arms. I'd like to invite up Mr. Tolbert, Mr. Sean Khorsandi, Mr. Turan, and Ms. Peg Breen. Okay. Thank you. I'm going to go from the left to the right. You can start.

Good morning, Council Members and Chair Ung. My name is Frampton Tolbert. I'm an Executive Director of the Historic Districts Council, the citywide advocacy organization for New York's historic neighborhoods. We collaborate and represent more than 500 community partner organizations, helping preserve the places that matter to them. We are here to testify today on the nomination of Lisa Kersavage as Chair of the

COMMITTEE ON RULES, PRIVILEGES, ELECTIONS, STANDARDS AND ETHICS 74 Landmarks Preservation Commission. HCC has worked with the nominee for many years in her role at the LPC, as well as at other institutions such as the Municipal Art Society and Friends of the Upper East Side. We think this role does require formal preservation knowledge and experience and are pleased to see someone with that experience nominated. We look forward to working with the Chair to further preservation across the city, especially in communities that have been overlooked and are less invested in by the LPC. We urge the City Council to make sure that the LPC is carrying out its duty to designate the places that matter. In the previous mayoral administration, designations fell dramatically and we lost significant places like the Pennsylvania Hotel and 270 Park Avenue to name just two that could have been retained and repurposed for housing or other uses. We also ask that the LPC provide more transparency in decision-making around its equity framework, which aims to ensure a fair representation of New York City's diverse history. There are many communities that still do not feel their neighborhoods have been adequately represented in landmark designations, East Harlem, East New York,

COMMITTEE ON RULES, PRIVILEGES, ELECTIONS, STANDARDS AND ETHICS 75 Parkchester, Astoria, the Lower East Side, and Bayside to name just a few. Finally, I would ask that the City Council work with the LPC to make sure that preservation is part of the solution for the housing crisis in New York City. This includes both the preservation of existing housing, the numerous historic apartment buildings and tenements, as well as new housing. The LPC has approved numerous proposals for conversion of housing and new housing in historic districts, but in many ways has barely scratched the surface on what could be possible. Thank you for consideration of our remarks and we look forward to our continued work with the LPC in preserving New York City.

Good morning, Commissioners and Council Members. Sean Khorsandi for Landmark West. Over the years, we've had the pleasure of working with Lisa in her prior roles across a variety of landmarks issues. With Lisa, the City has an experienced official who understands the intricacies and flexibility of the Landmarks Law and can begin work day one. While her knowledge of the entire New

COMMITTEE ON RULES, PRIVILEGES, ELECTIONS, STANDARDS AND ETHICS 76 York City landmarks process is extensive, her ability to respond to special circumstances and preservation issues with extraordinary elan makes her an exceptional candidate. We've witnessed her commitment to addressing vulnerable buildings. The most vulnerable New York City landmark is West Park Presbyterian Church. We are confident that upon analysis of the facts, the reality of this self-imposed hardship will be clear to the Commission. Lisa has also worked to recognize underrepresented communities and typologies. We all know that landmark status can not only stabilize a community and protect affordability, but also bring socioeconomic benefits. It's important that underrepresented stories continue to be told. The West Side is home to a cacophony of architectural styles and typologies and diverse histories, many which remain unprotected. We have significant sites of urban renewal, including NYCHA's Amsterdam houses. Among the first post-war housing in Manhattan, the site first acquired first via eminent domain in order to clear historically Black and Puerto Rican neighborhood of San Juan Hill. Under the current White House Administration, modernism is under

COMMITTEE ON RULES, PRIVILEGES, ELECTIONS, STANDARDS AND ETHICS 77 attack. Despite having numerous modern structures within our boundary, one of the most significant modernist campuses, Lincoln Center, also unprotected. We have extant model tenements that bear witness to the evolution of housing reforms in the city, not protected. And the first of its typology, PS-165, architect C.B.J. Snyder's first use of the H Plan for public schools, which became the citywide standard, not protected. Despite success, there's still so much work to do to see designations that bear and reflect the true breadth of our diverse, dense, and deserving neighborhood. Lisa Kersavage possesses all the characteristics required for the Chair, her expertise, enthusiasm, intelligence, and objectivity. We look forward to working with her and the agency to achieve our mutual goals.

Good morning, Chair Ung and Committee Members. I'm Peg Breen, President of the New York Landmarks Conservancy. We're a 53-year-old preservation organization that works to save the city's architectural heritage through advocacy, loans, grants, and technical help to the owners of historic properties. Through the years, we've loaned

COMMITTEE ON RULES, PRIVILEGES, ELECTIONS, STANDARDS AND ETHICS 78 and granted almost 63 million dollars for preservation work.
